reference_method: Use the supplied long-reading problem/answer references together with the user's explicit minimum-rule page. Slash-reading is a left-to-right support translation. The minimum rule takes priority over older generic heuristics.

rules.rule: Minimum mandatory rule from the user-supplied page: insert a slash (1) before prepositions and conjunctions, (2) before infinitive to + base verb, and (3) after commas; translate chunk-by-chunk. Apply this as the floor across every passage, while preserving truly fixed multiword prepositional units when necessary for readability.
examples: I bought a book / which the doctor wrote.
We can use a furoshiki / as a bag / when we buy something!
I think / there are a lot of things / we can do / for the earth.
To use a furoshiki is just one / of them.
We should always have the word mottainai / in our minds / and think what we can do.

rules.rule: Use relatively fine meaning chunks so a learner can process the English from left to right. Long sentences should normally contain multiple slashes. Do not leave most longer sentences unsplit.
Time, place, duration and other readable adjuncts are often separate chunks.
examples: I visited America / last year / and stayed there / for two months.
I read books / at home / on Saturday, / and I went to see a movie, Love with Me, / on Sunday.
We practice / from Monday / to Saturday.

rules.rule: Purpose infinitives are commonly separated from the preceding core clause.
examples: I went to school / to study English.
I'm going to the playground / to practice soccer.
My sister is coming / to see me.

rules.rule: Because, if, when and similar subordinate clauses are separated when they form a clear reading unit, including clause-first structures.
examples: I'm glad to meet you / because you can speak English very well.
If you are interested, / you should go / on a weekday.
Well, / after you watch the game today, / if you like our team, / you can join us.

rules.rule: Coordinated clauses and major coordinated units are separated in accordance with the minimum conjunction rule and the reference examples.
examples: The movie is very popular, / so a lot of people go to see it / on the weekend.
It will start / at four, / and we will play / at our playground.
So, / I think, / about five or six days a week, / after school.

rules.rule: Prepositional phrases and passive-agent phrases are slash candidates under the minimum rule; do not impose a generic ban on splitting a predicate before a following prepositional phrase.
examples: I went to see it / with my friends.
The book was written / by a famous writer.
We saw many kinds of animals / from all over the world.

rules.rule: Reporting/thought verbs may be followed by a separate content-clause chunk.
examples: I didn't know / that there is a soccer team / in this school.
I think / I'm good at playing soccer / because I practiced hard.

rules.rule: Short discourse markers, greetings and response units are isolated when useful.
examples: Yes, / can I help you?
Also, / I'm in the English club / in this school.
Well, / I stayed at home / on Saturday / because it was raining.

rules.rule: Questions can be divided into time/place/vocative chunks.
examples: What did you do / last Sunday, / Kenta?
What did you do / on the weekend, / Tina?

rules.rule: The reference can separate a long subject or predicate/complement sequence for reading support; generic bans such as 'never split be + complement' are not authoritative.
examples: Playing in bad weather / isn't difficult / for me.

rules.rule: Do not invent meaningless divisions inside a short/simple sentence that contains no minimum-rule boundary and needs no extra chunk.
examples: You speak English very well.
Have you ever played soccer?

rules.rule: Within one dialogue turn, slashes can separate complete neighboring sentences as well as sentence-internal chunks.
examples: I'm his brother. / My name is Paul. / Nice to meet you.

rules.rule: Japanese support text must correspond chunk-for-chunk in the same left-to-right order; it is separate from the natural full translation.
Do not use a fixed word-count interval. Apply the minimum boundary rules and reference-derived reading units.

benchmark_examples.english: Thank you. / I visited America / last year / and stayed there / for two months.
I went to school / to study English. / Also, / I'm in the English club / in this school.
What did you do / last Sunday, / Kenta?
If you are interested, / you should go / on a weekday. / The movie is very popular, / so a lot of people go to see it / on the weekend.
benchmark_examples.purpose: if clause + main clause + time + result coordination + time

benchmark_examples.english: The book was written / by a famous writer.
I played soccer / at school / in Canada / for three years.
I didn't know / that there is a soccer team / in this school.
Playing in bad weather / isn't difficult / for me.
